I have still not answered your letter of 23 February.
I want to tell you quite openly why.

You tell me of your conversion to the Catholic Church, and one cannot simply receive such news in silence. But neither is it easy to say anything substantial about it. For me, the Catholic faith is the religion of my fathers.
I am Catholic not only by confession, but by historical descent as well—if I may put it this way, by race.

I have watched a number of friends and acquaintances turn toward Catholicism and finally convert to it, beginning with Theodor Haecker in 1916 and continuing all the way to fellow prisoners in the camp in 1946.
Often, especially when I had unintentionally helped lead someone toward the practical conclusion, I felt like a brother who sees a long-lost friend return as the bridegroom of his sister.
For that reason, as in other cases of conversion, I find it impossible to make anything except the most private comments on an event of this kind.
Should I use some conventional family phrase of congratulations in your case? That would suit a lawyer speaking to another lawyer least of all.

What did Hobbes actually say and do? He courageously drew the consequences and organized them into a system. He was a thinker who accepted the given realities as given. But he was no enfant terrible like Max Stirner. Nor was he an opportunist. Nor a liar. Nor someone who supplied fig leaves. I read Sohm’s chapter on the Titulus (Church Law II, p. 284 ff., §29) with enormous excitement. It is a treasure house for the problems of declarations of invalidity, the revocability of acts of government, the irrevocability of administrative acts, retroactive effect, vested rights, and so on.

Church law—and the history of church law—really does prove richer, at least for a public-law scholar, and more powerful as a source of paradigmatic forms and models than the thoroughly privatized study of traditional Roman law.
